title: Intermittent Fasting NZ
meta_desc: Discover the benefits and risks of intermittent fasting for NZ gym-goers, with practical advice on 16:8, training windows, and affordable protein sources.
intro: Intermittent fasting has gained popularity in New Zealand, but is it suitable for everyone, especially those who regularly train at the gym? This guide will explore the pros and cons of intermittent fasting, including the 16:8 method, and provide actionable tips for NZ gym-goers. With input from NZ dietitians, we'll examine the impact on muscle loss, performance, and overall health.

sections.heading: What is Intermittent Fasting?
sections.body: Intermittent fasting involves alternating periods of eating and fasting in order to promote weight loss, improve metabolic health, and extend lifespan. The 16:8 method, which involves fasting for 16 hours and eating within an 8-hour window, is a popular choice among NZ gym-goers. For example, skipping breakfast and only eating between noon and 8 pm. Local supermarkets like Countdown and New World offer a range of healthy food options to support this eating pattern, including fresh produce, lean proteins, and whole grains.
list: 16:8 method: fast for 16 hours, eat within 8 hours
5:2 diet: eat normally for 5 days, restrict calories to 500-600 on the other 2 days
Eat-Stop-Eat: fast for 24 hours once or twice a week

sections.heading: Training Windows and Muscle Loss Risk
sections.body: When it comes to training, the timing of your workouts can be crucial when following an intermittent fasting regimen. NZ dietitians recommend scheduling your training sessions during your eating window to ensure you have sufficient energy and can refuel afterwards. This can help mitigate the risk of muscle loss. Additionally, incorporating affordable protein sources like chicken breast ($8.99/kg at Pak'nSave), fish, and eggs, as well as supplements like whey protein powder ($30-$50 per kilo), can support muscle growth and repair.
list: Schedule workouts during your eating window
Refuel with protein and complex carbohydrates after training
Consider adding supplements like creatine or HMB to support muscle growth

sections.heading: Performance Impact and Who IF Suits
sections.body: Intermittent fasting can have both positive and negative effects on athletic performance, depending on the individual and the specific regimen. Some NZ gym-goers may find that IF improves their mental clarity and focus, while others may experience decreased energy levels and reduced endurance. IF is not suitable for everyone, particularly those with a history of eating disorders, certain medical conditions, or who are underweight. Pregnant or breastfeeding women should also consult with their healthcare provider before starting any new diet or fasting regimen.
list: Increased fat burning and weight loss
Potential negative impacts on reproductive health and immune function

sections.heading: NZ Dietitian Consensus and Affordable Nutrition
sections.body: NZ dietitians generally agree that intermittent fasting can be a useful tool for weight loss and improving metabolic health, but it's essential to approach it in a balanced and sustainable way. This includes listening to your body, staying hydrated, and prioritising whole, nutrient-dense foods. Affordable nutrition options are available at local supermarkets, including seasonal produce, whole grains, and lean protein sources. Exercise NZ's subsidised gym scheme can also help make regular exercise more accessible, with discounts of 40-70% off gym memberships.
list: Stay hydrated and listen to your body
Consider consulting with a registered NZ dietitian for personalised advice

sections.heading: Getting Started with IF and Gym Training
sections.body: If you're considering trying intermittent fasting, start by assessing your current diet and training routine. Identify areas where you can make adjustments to support your goals, and consult with a healthcare professional or registered dietitian if needed. Begin with a gentle approach, such as the 12:12 method, and gradually increase your fasting window as your body adapts. Don't forget to stay hydrated, listen to your body, and prioritise rest and recovery.
